title: What is universal design for learning?
description: Universal design for learning (UDL) designs learning for variability from the start. CAST's three principles, the Guidelines 3.0 update, and workplace uses.
shortAnswer: A universal design for learning (UDL) approach designs learning environments to work for the full range of learners from the start, instead of retrofitting adjustments later. Developed by the nonprofit CAST, it rests on three principles: provide multiple means of engagement, multiple means of representation, and multiple means of action and expression. The CAST UDL Guidelines turn those principles into concrete design considerations; version 3.0 was released on July 30, 2024.
keyTakeaways: UDL changes the design of the learning environment rather than treating difficulty as a deficit in the learner.
Its three principles cover the why (engagement), the what (representation) and the how (action and expression) of learning.
CAST released the first UDL Guidelines in 2008; Guidelines 3.0, released July 30, 2024, is the fifth iteration.
Version 3.0 adds a focus on barriers rooted in biases and systems of exclusion, for learners with and without disabilities.
US federal law defines UDL in the Higher Education Act, as a framework that provides flexibility and reduces barriers while keeping high expectations.

sections.heading: What are the three principles of universal design for learning?

blocks.text: The three principles are engagement, representation, and action and expression. CAST's [UDL Guidelines FAQ](https://udlguidelines.cast.org/more/frequently-asked-questions/) describes them as the "why" of learning (how learners engage), the "what" (how they perceive information) and the "how" (how they act on and express what they know). Version 3.0 also emphasizes learners' identities, the "who" of learning, across all three.

Each principle is broken into guidelines, and each guideline into considerations. The [CAST UDL Guidelines 3.0](https://udlguidelines.cast.org/) graphic organizer arranges them in three rows: access, support, and executive function. CAST states the goal of UDL is learner agency that is "purposeful & reflective, resourceful & authentic, strategic & action-oriented."

sections.heading: What do the UDL Guidelines 3.0 contain?

blocks.text: The Guidelines contain nine guidelines, three per principle, each with design considerations. The table lists them with an original example of how each might apply in workplace training.

rows: Scenarios drawn from learners' actual roles and sites
State why the training matters, and give action-oriented feedback on practice

blocks.text: The numbering is out of order for historical reasons. CAST's FAQ explains that version 2.1 in 2014 moved engagement to the first position to highlight its role in learning, but the original numbers were kept.

sections.heading: How have the UDL Guidelines changed over time?

blocks.text: CAST released the first version of the Guidelines in 2008 and has revised them several times; Guidelines 3.0, released on July 30, 2024, is the fifth iteration. CAST began the update in 2020 and describes 3.0 as focused "specifically on addressing barriers rooted in biases and systems of exclusion for learners with and without disabilities."

The FAQ notes that earlier versions focused on barriers related to ability and disability, such as information presented only in printed text, while 3.0 extends this to barriers such as curriculum that does not represent a diversity of perspectives and identities. Version 2.2 remains available on CAST's downloads page for those who need it.

sections.heading: How does UDL relate to accessibility law and standards?

blocks.text: UDL is a design framework, not an accessibility standard, but it is recognized in some law. In the United States, the Higher Education Act definitions at [20 U.S.C. 1003(24)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/20/1003) define universal design for learning as "a scientifically valid framework for guiding educational practice" that provides flexibility in how information is presented, how students respond, and how they are engaged, and that "reduces barriers in instruction" while maintaining high achievement expectations.

Accessibility standards set minimum technical requirements for content; UDL goes further by designing choice and flexibility into the learning itself. In practice, organizations apply both: technical accessibility so everyone can use the material, and UDL so the design works for varied learners. See [how to make e-learning accessible](/guides/how-to-make-elearning-accessible).

sections.heading: How can UDL be applied to compliance and workplace training?

blocks.text: UDL applies by offering flexibility in how content is presented and how competence is shown, while keeping the standard itself fixed. That last point matters in regulated settings: options must not lower the requirement being assessed.

items: Offer the same content in more than one format, such as video with transcript and a short written summary.
Let experienced staff show existing competence instead of sitting through the full course, consistent with [recognition of prior learning](/glossary/recognition-of-prior-learning).
Allow different evidence formats where they show the same skill, while keeping the decision rule unchanged; see [rules of evidence](/glossary/rules-of-evidence).
Reduce unnecessary load first; UDL options work best on top of clear design, as described in [cognitive load theory](/glossary/cognitive-load-theory).
Use plain language, define regulatory terms, and connect new procedures to what learners already know.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry separates what must be learned and assessed, defined in the framework, from how content is presented. That separation lets the same outcome and evidence requirement be delivered in several formats without changing the standard learners must meet.

faqs.q: Is UDL only for learners with disabilities?
faqs.a: No. UDL is designed for the variability found in every group of learners. CAST describes it as a framework for learning that is accessible, inclusive, equitable and challenging for every learner, and version 3.0 explicitly addresses barriers for learners with and without disabilities. Designs that help some learners often help many.

faqs.q: Does UDL mean offering every option to every learner?
faqs.a: No. The Guidelines are considerations, not a checklist to complete in full. CAST notes there is no set order in which to apply them. Designers choose the options that remove the most significant barriers for their learners and goals, while keeping the learning outcome the same.

faqs.q: What brain networks is UDL based on?
faqs.a: CAST links the three principles to three broad networks: affective networks for engagement, recognition networks for perceiving information, and strategic networks for planning and action. CAST describes this as a simplified model used to understand and plan for learner variability, not a precise map of how learning works.
